title: The Aesthetic Appreciation of Ruins

findings.antecedent: A ruin (defined as: remains of a large-scale human-built physical structure incorporating architectural elements designed to last for a significant period of time, in the process of decay, showing age-value through nature's encroachment or altered use-value, and creating a new, unauthored aesthetic unity)
findings.consequent: aesthetic appreciation
findings.quote: A ruin is the remains of a large-scale human-built physical structure which... creates, through the process of its decay, a new, unauthored aesthetic unity.

findings.consequent: Appropriate model of aesthetic appreciation
findings.quote: the classification of an object, in this case a ruin, importantly informs our aesthetic appreciation of it.

findings.antecedent: Ruin being in the process of decay
findings.consequent: Deep aesthetic appreciation of ruins qua ruins
findings.quote: a person engaging with a ruin who brackets the fact that the ruin is in the process of decay will not have fully appreciated the ruin qua ruin.

findings.consequent: Rich aesthetic experiences
findings.quote: Thinking of ruins as mementos mori and as elicitors of the sublime addresses the fact that ruins focus our attention in interesting ways on the past, present, and future. These approaches can certainly work can together to provide us with rich aesthetic experiences.

findings.antecedent: Ruins as hybrid objects (part artifactual, part natural) and their tripartite nature
findings.consequent: Need for a pluralist account of aesthetic appreciation
findings.quote: The tripartite nature of ruins seems to call out for a pluralist response. As hybrid objects they “escape the standard theories.” Their nature (as both artifactual and natural) makes them ideal candidates for pluralist models.

findings.consequent: Preservation of unique aesthetic value of ruins
findings.quote: I believe managed decline is our best option to preserve what is uniquely compelling about ruins, it is the position that follows from ontology based aesthetic pluralism.

findings.antecedent: Removal of immovable cultural material from its in situ environment (e.g., kalan from Mỹ Sơn site)
findings.consequent: Destruction of aesthetic integrity and ontological shift (from ruin to sculpture)
findings.quote: When we take an object out of its environment, we change the object and consequently change the way we engage with it. As Balachandran says, the object (the ruin in this case) is obviously transformed physically... But further, and perhaps more importantly, we symbolically transform the object from ruin – an object in the process of decay and inextricably wedded to its environment –into a sculpture.

findings.consequent: Exploitation of local populations and cultural heritage
findings.quote: Ruth Sample asserts that exploitation is a failure to respect the inherent value in a person or thing. This lack of respect amounts to degradation.

findings.consequent: Misrepresentation of the city and its inhabitants (metonymic use)
findings.quote: Leary, in “Detroitism,” calls this the metonymic use of ruin porn. The photographs, these critics suppose, stand in for Detroit, and do so poorly.

findings.antecedent: Local Detroiters running ruin tours, contextualizing neighborhoods and buildings, funneling profits back to community
findings.consequent: Mitigation of exploitation worries in ruin tourism
findings.quote: Locals should have a chance to represent themselves and help create narratives about Detroit. Ruin tours should be operated and run by local Detroiters, who could fight against the metonymic use of Detroit ruin porn. Profits from these tours could be used to assist Detroiters.

findings.consequent: Aesthetic potential of a modern ruin actualized
findings.quote: Gas Works Park is an example in which the aesthetic potential of a modern ruin has been actualized.

findings.consequent: Elicitation of sublime experience
findings.quote: I believe the gas plants evoke something powerful that is hard to analyze, the feeling of the sublime.

findings.antecedent: Comparison of gas works to modern art (Rothko paintings, Tinguely sculptures)
findings.consequent: Local population's appreciation of gas works' beauty
findings.quote: In comparing the gas works to the paintings of Rothko and sculptures of Tinguely, Haag was able to get people to open their eyes to the beauty of the gas works.

findings.consequent: Provision of future generations with opportunity for unique aesthetic experiences
findings.quote: By keeping the ruinated gas works a ruin (through ruin stabilization) we have provided (at least close) future generations an opportunity to experience its unique beauty.

findings.antecedent: Ruins (as objects in process of decay, with tripartite nature)
findings.consequent: Elicitation of sublime and memento mori experiences
findings.quote: This tripartite nature is manifest when we see ruins as elicitors of the sublime and as power experiences of memento mori.

findings.consequent: Distinction from architectural cousins (intended structures)
findings.quote: ruins are aesthetically unintended (and therefore distinct from their architectural cousins).

findings.consequent: Aesthetic feature (in aesthetic frame)
findings.quote: Genuineness, she asserts, is a necessary condition for age value. Korsmeyer states, “the agedness of the historical artifact – an aspect of this stone wall that is the best candidate for being the closest continuer in the preservation of old Warsaw’s identity through time – is in the aesthetic frame.”

findings.antecedent: Viewing ruins in the present tense (focus on what is actually there)
findings.consequent: Increased accessibility to those without historical knowledge
findings.quote: focusing on what is present on the ground has the benefit of increased accessibility to those who don’t have the requisite historical knowledge, because those who don’t have the historical knowledge can still have a rich aesthetic experience of the elements that remain.

findings.consequent: Multisensory experience (touch, smell, sound)
findings.quote: As hybrid objects that contain both artifactual and natural elements, there is even more for us to touch, to move in and around, and to smell.

findings.consequent: Affect on how we see it as a ruin and fit its definition
findings.quote: Does classifying something as a ruin affect the way we see it as a ruin? Does classifying something as a ruin help us see it fit the definition of a ruin better? In my view, the answer to these questions is “Yes.”

findings.antecedent: Social factors (e.g., lack of human appreciation, protection, intervention)
findings.consequent: Causal role in a structure becoming a ruin
findings.quote: I think it is just as reasonable to argue that it was the lack of human appreciation, protection, and intervention that (partially) caused the castle to fall into ruin.

findings.antecedent: A ruin (as a distinct ontological entity from its original building)
findings.consequent: Possession of a new aesthetic unity
findings.quote: the ruin is a discrete aesthetic object from that of its purely architectural cousin. The aesthetic focus often evokes references to both the future and the past.

findings.consequent: Aesthetic unintendedness
findings.quote: First, he states that ruins are, for the most part, aesthetically unintended. He does not, however, give us an example of intended ruins, and I will argue that, except in one particular case, ruins are not aesthetically intended.

findings.consequent: Historical importance and cultural associations
findings.quote: Ruins often reflect a history abounding with cultural associations and historical relations. The historical ties ruins have will often place them in the category of ‘cultural property.’

findings.consequent: Esteemed age-value (through perseverance)
findings.quote: Even in the case of new ruins, the ruin expresses this age-value through perseverance.

findings.consequent: Change in use-value (from functional to aesthetic/historical)
findings.quote: When a decayed arsenal (such as Bannerman’s) no longer can complete its primary function it is often seen as useless. If my arsenal cannot keep my weapons stored safely, then what use is it? Edensor and I argue that if the arsenal is understood as a ruin, its use-value has not diminished, but has merely changed.

findings.consequent: Aesthetic unity distinct from its merely artifactual cousin
findings.quote: When we look at a ruin, we admire something above and beyond its mere architectural structure. We see this distinction being made by Hetzler, Crawford, and Ginsberg.

findings.consequent: Multisensory experience (touch, hear, taste, smell)
findings.quote: These landscape values can be purely aesthetic, by which I mean “narrowly aesthetic” – or having only to do with the senses (i.e., what one can immediately see, touch, hear, taste, or smell).

findings.consequent: Aesthetic appreciation (variety of modes)
findings.quote: ruins remain important objects of aesthetic appreciation due in part to the variety of modes of appreciation one might employ in engaging with them

findings.consequent: Aesthetic fascination
findings.quote: My goal is to explain our peculiar aesthetic fascination with architectural ruins and to show why ruins are worthy of our time and aesthetic appreciation.

findings.consequent: More appealing than non-ruinated aesthetic cousins (emergent properties)
findings.quote: emergent properties of ruinated structures can make them more appealing than their non-ruinated aesthetic cousins.

findings.antecedent: Intention behind a ruination (e.g., aesthetic qualities, political position, lack of funds)
findings.consequent: Aesthetic appraisal of the ruin
findings.quote: I will argue that the intention behind a ruination can affect its aesthetic appraisal.

findings.consequent: Express age-value through perseverance
findings.quote: Even in the case of new ruins, the ruin expresses this age-value through perseverance.

findings.consequent: Multisensory experience (sounds, smells)
findings.quote: There are sounds (e.g., echoes) smells (e.g., mold, must, wild flowers). Ruins retain power because they seem resistant to time.

findings.antecedent: Classical conception of ruin appreciation (ruin as data for reconstruction)
findings.consequent: Undue restriction of aesthetic appreciation focus
findings.quote: I also argued that this way of appreciating ruins unduly restricts the focus of our aesthetic appreciation.

findings.consequent: Importance of historical information for aesthetic appreciation
findings.quote: From the classical model we have learned that historical information importantly informs the aesthetic appreciation of ruins

findings.consequent: Better capture of unique aesthetic appreciation of ruins than picturesque
findings.quote: Finally, I assert that while the picturesque is more often associated with ruin appreciation, the sublime might be a more accurate category.

findings.consequent: Powerful cultural artifacts worthy of advocacy and preservation (stabilization)
findings.quote: Maybe one of the most important lessons Gas Works Park has taught us is that modern ruin are powerful cultural artifacts, worthy of advocacy and preservation (i.e., ruin stabilization).

findings.consequent: Destruction of authenticity and conveyance of erroneous information
findings.quote: I argue that to reconstruct is always to destroy some measure of authenticity. To preserve authenticity one must leave the object more or less alone... When ruins are reconstructed, they provide a false face to their witnesses. They lie about their age value and ability to stand the test of time.

findings.consequent: Preservation of its conceptual integrity
findings.quote: In order to preserve the conceptual integrity of the ruin, one must allow it to continue this process – allowing the architectural structure a finite lifespan.

findings.consequent: Evocation of the sublime (feelings of awe and respect toward creation of man and vastness of nature)
findings.quote: However ruins seem much more powerful as symbols for the dynamical sublime, as they evoke feelings of awe and respect toward both the creation of man and the vastness of nature.

findings.consequent: Mementos mori (ruminating on mortality, fleeting nature of life)
findings.quote: The sense that nature reabsorbs even the most permanent-seeming structures helps man to ruminate on his own mortality and the fleeting nature of life in general. Ruins are ephemerality writ large.

findings.antecedent: Social construction of the concept of ruins
findings.consequent: Ability to change the concept and its associated practices
findings.quote: When we know a concept is socially constructed, we know it can be changed; it no longer is part of the natural order of things.

findings.antecedent: Local and descendant communities having control over cultural heritage
findings.consequent: Social ontology of ruins (communities deeming structures as ruins)
findings.quote: Finally, the motivation for a social ontology of ruins comes from wanting descendant and local communities to have control over their own cultural heritage.

findings.consequent: Multisensory experience (touch)
findings.quote: engaging with a ruin in situ is a multi-sensory experience that may (or should) involve touch.

findings.consequent: Preclusion of aesthetic appreciation (in some cases)
findings.quote: This much discussed example shows that knowledge sometimes precludes aesthetic appreciation.

findings.antecedent: Viewing nature as picturesque (as landscape painting)
findings.consequent: Incomplete and shallow aesthetic engagement with natural environment
findings.quote: This leads us to have an incomplete and shallow aesthetic engagement with the natural environment, since we are not engaging with the multi-sensory, multi-dimensional ingredients of nature.

findings.consequent: Hybrid objects (part artifactual, part natural)
findings.quote: Second, a ruin is an ontologically curious object because it clearly bridges the artifactual / natural divide. Because a ruin is hybrid: partly built by humans and partly created by nature

findings.consequent: Aesthetic appreciation (worthwhile pursuit, pleasure)
findings.quote: I hope I have succeeded in convincing you that ruin contemplation is very much alive today, and that discovering ruins’ meaning and encountering their beauty is a worthwhile pursuit, a pleasure that can span a lifetime.

limitations: The monism/pluralism debate will not be settled in this dissertation (p. 134).
The account focuses on architectural ruins, but could be extended to shipwrecks and gardens (p. 216).
The discussion of the picturesque has been simplified (p. 114, footnote 168).
The definition of ruins is not 'hard and fast' due to the sorites paradox (p. 34, 127).
The 'everything goes' criticism of pluralism is not fully addressed (p. 134).
The discussion of the sublime is preliminary (p. 131).
The distinction between romantic ruin appreciation and romantic ruin-art is important (p. 152).
The account does not provide an account of what makes one ruin more beautiful than another (p. 139, footnote 221).
minimum_safe_summary: This dissertation proposes a model of aesthetic appreciation specific to architectural ruins, arguing that ruins are ontologically curious hybrid objects that are partially constituted by their communities viewing them as such. The author defines a ruin as a large-scale human-built physical structure in the process of decay, showing age-value and creating a new, unauthored aesthetic unity. Key findings include that the ontological status of a ruin informs its aesthetic appreciation, which should be pluralistic and encompass the ruin's tripartite nature (past, present, and future), often eliciting feelings of the sublime and memento mori. The author advocates for 'managed decline' as an ethical preservation strategy, allowing decay while ensuring safety and accessibility, and critiques exploitative 'ruin porn' tourism in modern contexts like Detroit. Limitations include not fully resolving the monism/pluralism debate and focusing primarily on architectural ruins.
